Significant Accomplishments and Conclusions: A novel encapsulating electrode was formed using a highly transparent and conductive composite (TCC) coated with a sputtered indium zinc oxide (IZO) thin film (Figure 27a). Facile monolithic integration of the IZO/TCC structure onto the perovskite solar cell (PSC) was achieved without any loss in PCE. An encapsulated PSC maintained above 90% of its initial power conversion efficiency of 21.65% for up to 1,430 hours, compared to less than 300 hours for an unencapsulated control (Figure 27b). The result obtained in this project (PCE 21.65%: T90 of 1,430 hours) demonstrates the highest performance amongst thin-film encapsulated PSCs aged under illumination in air with MPP-tracking (Figure 27c), on par with the historical trend of operational stabilities achieved with all encapsulation techniques.3 Despite the focus on PV testing using PSCs grown on rigid SLG substrates, the TCC-based encapsulating electrode is adaptable to other modes of operations, including flexible PV and photoelectrochemical water-splitting devices. Such a system provides the element of “added functionality” to the triad of low-cost, efficient, and stable characteristics desired in next-generation PV technologies. With further refinement, TCC can pave the way for improved passivation and encapsulation techniques for use in thin-film photovoltaic and photoelectrochemical devices. 40/52 DE-EE0010241 Nicolas Gaillard Figure 27: (a) Concept image of an IZO/TCC/PSC sample. The National Renewable Energy Laboratory received $100,000 directly from DOE to support the program with PSCs manufacturing, testing and WVTR measurements on free-standing TCCs. The project started on September 1, 2022, and ended on March 1, 2024. However, we have been continuing work on publishing the project results at no cost to DOE; we submitted a journal manuscript on May 1st, 2025. 10.
